options: never breaks symmetry: units stay copies of each other
check.why: Same inputs, same blame, same updates, forever.

check.q: A ReLU layer has 32 inputs. He initialization uses weights with standard deviation…

goals: Recognize overfitting from train vs validation error
Use train/validation/test splits and cross-validation honestly
Regularize, and know when more data is the real fix
cards: Fitting the training data's noise: low training error, high error on new data.
Fit on train, choose on validation, report on test, touched once.
Rotate which slice is the validation set; average the scores. For small datasets.
Add λ·Σw² to the loss: big weights cost, so the fit bends less.
Error vs training-set size: a big train–validation gap means more data will help.
Information from validation/test (or the future) sneaking into training, e.g. scaling or selecting features on all data.

check.q: Training error 0.01, validation error 0.40. The model is…
check.why: Great on what it saw, bad on new data.

check.q: You tried 50 settings and picked the best by validation score. Its validation score is…
options: an unbiased estimate of new-data error
optimistic: that's why a separate test set exists
check.why: Choosing the best of many is itself a fit to the validation set.

check.q: Raising the ridge λ makes the model…
check.why: Big weights cost more, so the curve bends less.

check.q: Train and validation error are both high and close together. More data will…
options: barely help: the model is too simple
check.why: That's high bias: you need a more flexible model or better features.

check.q: Feature selection on all the data, then cross-validation, reports 75% on random noise. Why?
options: Leakage: the selection already saw every fold's labels
check.why: Put every data-dependent step inside the pipeline.

check.q: Why does the validation error rise again as the degree keeps growing, while the training error keeps falling?
options: The extra flexibility fits this sample's noise (variance), and new points carry different noise
Because high-degree polynomials can't be fit by least squares
Because the validation set is too small to measure anything
check.why: Expected error = noise + bias² + variance. More degree lowers bias but raises variance; past the bottom of the U, variance wins.

goals: Read a confusion matrix and compute precision and recall
Compare models across thresholds with ROC and precision-recall curves
Choose a threshold by cost and check calibration
cards: Of the cases flagged, the share that were real: TP / (TP + FP).
Of the real cases, the share caught: TP / (TP + FN).
With rare positives, 'always no' scores high accuracy and catches nothing.
The chance a random positive scores above a random negative; 0.5 is a coin flip.
Pick the cutoff that minimizes cost of false negatives + false positives, not 0.5 by default.
Does a predicted 0.8 come true 80% of the time? Check with a calibration curve.

check.q: A fraud model flags 10 payments; 4 are fraud, and there were 8 frauds in total. Precision and recall?
check.why: Precision 4/10, recall 4/8.

check.q: Fraud is 1 in 1000. 'Never fraud' has accuracy…
check.why: And recall 0: accuracy hides it.

check.q: Lowering the threshold usually…
check.why: You flag more: catch more, but with more false alarms.

check.q: Misses cost 20× more than false alarms. The best threshold is probably…
check.why: Accept more false alarms to avoid costly misses.

check.q: A model says 0.8 for many cases; 55% of them turn out positive. It is…
check.why: Its probabilities run higher than reality.

check.q: Why does precision fall when fraud gets rarer, while recall stays the same?
options: Recall is measured only on frauds, but precision mixes in false alarms from the honest crowd, which grows as fraud gets rarer
Because the model gets worse on rare data
Because the threshold moves on its own
check.why: Same false-positive rate on more honest payments means more false alarms per real hit. That's the base-rate trap.

goals: Explain how a decision tree splits and why deep trees overfit
Explain bagging (random forests) and boosting
Pick between linear models and boosted trees for tabular data
cards: A sequence of yes/no questions on features; each leaf predicts an average or a majority.
Its complexity knob: deep trees memorize the training data.
Average many deep trees grown on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets; errors partly cancel.
Add small trees one at a time, each fitting what the model still gets wrong (the residuals).
Stop adding trees when a held-out score stops improving.
Shuffle one feature and measure how much worse the model gets.

check.q: A tree with unlimited depth on noisy data will…
check.why: Each leaf ends up holding one point.

check.q: In gradient boosting, each new tree is trained on…
options: a random half of the features
what the current model still gets wrong
check.why: It fits the residuals (for squared error).

check.q: Why does boosting use a small learning rate like 0.1?
options: So each tree only nudges, and many small steps generalize better
check.why: Small steps with many trees, stopped early, overfit less.

check.q: For a tabular dataset with mixed features and nonlinear effects, a strong first choice is…
check.why: Boosted trees win most tabular problems with little tuning.

check.q: What should you always fit before any fancy model?
options: A baseline (the mean, or a linear model)
check.why: Without a baseline you can't tell if the fancy model helps.

goals: Build and interpret confidence intervals
Run a hypothesis test and read a p-value correctly
Compare two models fairly and plan an A/B test's size
cards: A method that catches the true value in 95% of samples: x̄ ± t·s/√n.
How often noise alone would produce a gap this big if there were no real difference.
False alarm (rate α) / missed real effect (rate β); power = 1 − β.
Compare them on the same test examples; only disagreements carry information (McNemar).
Checking repeatedly and stopping at p < 0.05 inflates false positives far above 5%.

check.q: A 95% interval is [48, 52]. Which is right?
options: 95% chance the true mean is in it
95% of intervals built this way contain the true mean
95% of the data is in it
check.why: The 95% describes the method.

check.q: p = 0.03 means…
options: a 3% chance the null is true
if there were no difference, a gap this big would happen about 3% of the time
check.why: It's computed assuming the null is true.

check.q: Two models are scored on the same test set. The right test is…
options: a paired test on the disagreements
check.why: Pairing cancels the shared difficulty of examples.

check.q: Doubling the sample size makes the margin of error…
check.why: Margins shrink like 1/√n.

check.q: You check an A/B test daily and stop at the first p < 0.05. The false-positive rate is…
check.why: Each look is another chance for noise to cross the line.

check.q: Why does detecting a lift half as large need about four times the visitors?
options: The standard error shrinks like 1/√n, so halving the gap you can see means doubling √n, which is four times n
Because smaller effects need a smaller α
Because the p-value halves when n doubles
check.why: n ≈ 16 p(1 − p)/δ²: δ is squared in the denominator.

goals: See an image as a grid of numbers and a filter as a small sliding pattern
Compute a convolution, its output size and its parameter count
Explain why CNNs beat dense layers on images
cards: Slide a small filter over the image; at each spot multiply and add: one output number per position.
The grid of a filter's responses: bright where its pattern appears.
⌊(n + 2p − k)/s⌋ + 1 for input n, kernel k, padding p, stride s.
Keep the biggest value in each small block: smaller maps, small shifts don't matter.
One filter is reused at every position: few parameters, and a pattern is found wherever it is.
A filter spans all input channels (e.g. RGB); the number of filters is the output's depth.

check.q: An image is 28×28. A 3×3 filter, no padding, stride 1, gives a map of…
Where does a vertical-edge filter respond most?
options: Where brightness changes from left to right
check.why: Its left and right columns have opposite signs.

check.q: How many parameters in a 3×3 conv layer with 3 input channels and 64 filters?
check.why: 64 × 3 × 3 × 3 weights + 64 biases.

check.q: 2×2 max pooling turns a 14×14 map into…
check.why: Each 2×2 block becomes one number.

check.q: Why do CNNs need far fewer parameters than dense layers on images?
options: Each filter is shared across every position
check.why: Weight sharing: one small filter, applied everywhere.

goals: Find moving things by subtracting frames
Explain what a trained detector outputs: boxes, classes, confidences
Use IoU and non-maximum suppression to clean up detections
cards: Subtract two frames: pixels that changed a lot are moving things (or noise).
Group touching changed pixels into blobs, one per object (roughly).
A list of boxes, each with a class and a confidence.
Intersection over union of two boxes: 1 = identical, 0 = no overlap.
Keep the most confident box, drop boxes overlapping it heavily, repeat.
Higher means fewer, surer detections; lower catches more, with more mistakes.

check.q: Two equal boxes overlap by half their width. Their IoU is…
check.why: Intersection 1/2, union 3/2 (in box areas): 1/3.

check.q: A detector returns three overlapping boxes on one car. NMS keeps…
check.why: The others overlap it heavily and get dropped.

check.q: Why does frame differencing show a moving car as two blobs?
options: Only the car's front and back change; its middle is bright in both frames
check.why: Compare against an empty-road background instead.

check.q: Raising the confidence threshold makes the counts…
check.why: Fewer boxes pass a stricter cutoff.

check.q: COCO-trained detectors know…
check.why: They're trained on COCO's 80 categories.

goals: Treat words as vectors and compare them by cosine similarity
Compute scaled dot-product attention with queries, keys and values
Assemble a transformer block: attention, MLP, residuals, layer norm
cards: A vector of numbers per token; similar meanings point in similar directions.
Each token asks (query), advertises (key), and offers content (value); weights come from query·key.
softmax(QKᵀ/√d)·V: every token becomes a weighted mix of the values.
Dot products grow like √d; without scaling, softmax gets nearly one-hot and gradients vanish.
Set future positions' scores to −∞ so a token can't look ahead: needed to predict the next token.
x + attention(norm(x)), then x + MLP(norm(x)): same shape in and out, stacked many times.

check.q: In attention, the weights in each row…
check.why: Each token's output is a weighted average of the values.

check.q: Why is there a causal mask in a GPT?
options: So a token can't see the tokens it should predict
check.why: Training predicts each next token, so later tokens must stay hidden.

check.q: Attention scores are divided by √d because…
options: dot products grow with dimension, which would make softmax too peaked
check.why: Random dot products have spread √d.

check.q: Without positional information, attention treats a sentence as…
options: a bag of tokens: order is invisible
check.why: Swap two tokens and attention can't tell, so positions are added.

check.q: The residual connection in a block means…
options: the layer's output is added to its input
check.why: x + f(x): easy to keep information and train deep stacks.

goals: Frame language modeling as predicting the next token
Build and train a tiny GPT
Sample from it with temperature, and spot memorization
cards: A model of P(next token | previous tokens); generating = sampling one token at a time.
Each character is a token: a tiny vocabulary, long sequences.
How many previous tokens the model can see.
The input shifted by one: every position predicts the next token.
Divide the scores before softmax: low = safe and repetitive, high = creative and error-prone.
With a small dataset, long training makes the model reproduce its training examples.

check.q: A GPT is trained to…
options: predict the next token at every position
check.why: Generation is that prediction, repeated.

check.q: A model that knew nothing, with a 68-character vocabulary, would have a loss of about…
check.why: Uniform guessing: −ln(1/68).

check.q: Sampling at temperature 0.5 instead of 1.5 gives names that are…
options: safer and closer to common patterns
check.why: Low temperature sharpens the distribution toward likely characters.

check.q: After long training on 379 names, most samples are real station names. That's…
check.why: Hold out names and stop when validation loss stops falling.

check.q: Why does the model need position embeddings?
options: To know which character comes where
check.why: Attention alone ignores order.

goals: Write the agent loop: model → tool call → result → … → answer
Guard tools: validate arguments, return fixable errors
Measure an agent with an eval set, error bars and paired comparisons
cards: Send messages to the model; if it calls a tool, run it, append the result, repeat until it answers.
A tool's name, description and JSON schema of arguments: what the model sees and must follow.
Validate arguments, cap the rounds, refuse unknown tools, and return errors the model can fix.
The Model Context Protocol: JSON-RPC for agents to list and call tools on a server.
Many different labeled cases, written before tuning; measure with confidence intervals.
Run both on the same cases and use a paired test (McNemar).

check.q: The model asks for a tool that doesn't exist. The agent should…
options: return an error message to the model so it can recover
check.why: Errors are messages too.

check.q: Why validate a tool's arguments before running it?
options: Models sometimes invent fields or wrong types
check.why: Check first, and answer mistakes with a fixable error.

check.q: Why cap the number of rounds?
options: To save tokens and stop loops that never end
check.why: A confused model can call tools forever.

check.q: An eval of 20 cases shows 90%. A fair summary is…
options: about 90%, but plausibly anywhere from ~75% to ~100%
check.why: Small evals have wide error bars.

check.q: Two agent versions answered the same 200 questions. Compare them with…
options: a paired test on the disagreements
check.why: Same questions: pair them (McNemar).

goals: Name the pieces of a deployed model: input, preprocessing, model, postprocessing
Prepare an image the way a pretrained model expects
Turn scores into an honest answer and put a model on the web
cards: Input → preprocessing → model (architecture + saved weights) → postprocessing → interface.
Same size, scale and normalization as in training, ideally the same code (weights.transforms()).
Resize, center-crop 224, scale to 0–1, normalize per channel, shape (batch, 3, 224, 224).
Softmax the scores, show the top few labels with their probabilities.
A classifier always picks one of its labels, even for things it never saw.
Gradio wraps a Python function in a web page; Spaces hosts it for free from app.py + requirements.txt + model files.
One full pass over the training data.
The handful of examples used for one gradient step: cheaper than all of them, and the noise helps.
The rule that turns gradients into weight updates: plain gradient descent, momentum, Adam (stage 4 compares them).
The usual default optimizer: gradient descent with momentum and a per-weight step size; AdamW adds weight decay.
PyTorch's array: like a NumPy array, but it can live on a GPU and remembers how it was computed for backprop.
A processor with thousands of small cores: matrix products run tens of times faster than on a CPU.
A network already trained on a big dataset; fine-tuning trains it a little more on your task, usually with a new last layer.

check.q: The app feeds 0–255 pixels to a model trained on 0–1 inputs. The result is…
check.why: Nothing checks the range; the model just sees inputs it never learned.

check.q: How many numbers does a 224×224 RGB image become?
A pet-breed model gets a photo of a car. It will…
check.why: Softmax spreads 100% over the classes it knows.

check.q: When fine-tuning a pretrained network, the new last layer usually gets…
options: a smaller learning rate than the body
a bigger learning rate than the body
check.why: It starts from random; the pretrained body only needs gentle adjusting.

check.q: Which files does a Gradio Space need?
options: app.py, requirements.txt and the model files
check.why: Spaces installs the requirements and runs app.py.

check.q: Why must an app resize and normalize photos exactly the way training did?
options: The weights were tuned on numbers in that exact range and layout, so other inputs give the network numbers it has never seen
Because the model file stores the photo size and refuses others
check.why: Raw 0–255 pixels are hundreds of times bigger than normalized ones; the scores blow up and softmax picks a nonsense class, with no error message.

goals: Write the PyTorch training loop and say what each line does
Use tensors, nn.Module, Dataset and DataLoader the way production code does
Debug training with the habits: overfit one batch, the ln(classes) loss, eval() and no_grad()
cards: For each epoch, for each batch: forward, loss, zero_grad, backward, step.
One pass over all the training data.
The handful of examples behind one step; its gradient is a noisy guess of the full one.
.backward() adds to .grad; without clearing, each step mixes in all earlier gradients.
A layer or stack that owns its parameters: layers in __init__, the data flow in forward.
Switch before training and before measuring; evaluate inside with torch.no_grad().
A Dataset gives the length and the i-th example; a DataLoader shuffles and batches.
A model that can't drive one batch's loss to ~0 has a bug in the model or the loop.
The loss of uniform guessing (2.3 for 10 classes): stuck there means nothing is learning.
A recipe for objects: __init__ runs when one is made, self is the object, methods get self.
with X: switches X on for the indented block only, then off again.

check.q: With 50,000 training examples and a batch size of 100, how many optimizer steps are 3 epochs?
check.why: 500 batches per epoch × 3 epochs.

check.q: A training script forgets optimizer.zero_grad(). What happens?
options: Each step's gradient includes all earlier ones, so updates grow wrong and training goes haywire, with no error
check.why: .backward() adds into .grad (the right rule inside one pass); clearing between steps is your job.

check.q: In class MLP(nn.Module), what is self inside __init__?
options: The MLP object being made, so self.layers = ... stores the layers on it
check.why: self is the object; storing layers on it is how PyTorch finds their parameters.

check.q: Why does the test DataLoader usually not shuffle?
options: Measuring doesn't depend on order, so there's nothing to gain
Shuffling the test set would leak labels
check.why: Shuffling matters for training, where batch order shapes the gradient steps.

check.q: Your new 10-class model's loss sits at 2.30 and won't move, even on a single batch. Most likely?
options: A bug: nothing is being learned (a missing step or zero_grad, or a learning rate of 0)
check.why: ln 10 ≈ 2.30 is the loss of uniform guessing.

goals: Clean a table: sentinel codes, missing values, scaling, one-hot encoding
Build a pipeline that learns every preprocessing step from training rows only
Handle a rare class with stratified splits, class weights and thresholds
Spot and fix leakage: target leaks, time splits, group splits, preprocessing before the split
cards: A special value like 999 or −1 meaning 'none' or 'unknown': turn it into a flag column.
z = (x − mean) / std, with the mean and std from the training rows only.
Gradient descent, distances (kNN, clustering) and regularized models; trees don't.
One 0/1 column per category, so no fake order is invented.
Preprocessing + model as one object: fit learns everything from training rows; cross-validation refits it per fold.
class_weight='balanced' makes rare examples count more: recall up, precision down, ranking (AUC) about the same.
Information available while building the model that won't exist when it's used.
A column filled in after the outcome (call duration, treatment given): it knows the answer.
Train on the past, test on the later period, whenever data has time in it.
Keep each person, device or place entirely in train or entirely in test (GroupKFold).

check.q: The bank's pdays column uses 999 for 'never contacted'. What's the best fix for a linear model?
options: Add a 'contacted before' flag and stop treating 999 as a number of days
Leave it: 999 is far away, which is roughly right
check.why: 96% of rows are 999: deleting them throws away the data, and as a number it drags every average.

check.q: You standardize all 41,000 rows, then split into train and test. What's wrong?
options: The test rows helped set the mean and spread, so a little test information leaked into training
check.why: The leak is small for a scaler but large for feature selection or target encoding. A pipeline makes the habit automatic.

check.q: With 11% positives, class_weight='balanced' raises recall from 0.21 to 0.62. What happens to precision?
options: It falls: more people are flagged, and a smaller share of them are real yeses
check.why: Weighting moves the effective threshold; precision and recall trade off (chapter 12).

check.q: The interest rate alone scores AUC 0.77 on a random split and 0.50 on a time split. Why?
options: The rate changes over time, so it acts like a calendar: a random split lets the model look up how neighboring days went
The time split has too few rows
check.why: On a time split the test period has rates never seen in training, which is what launch day looks like.

check.q: A model predicting customer churn uses 'number of support tickets in the last 30 days', computed on the day the data was pulled, after the churn happened. Is that a problem?
options: Yes: it includes tickets filed after the moment of prediction, possibly about cancelling
No: support tickets are a real signal
Only if the classes are imbalanced
check.why: Rebuild the feature from what was known at prediction time: tickets in the 30 days before that moment.

check.q: Why does choosing columns on all the data before cross-validation score well even on pure noise?
options: The test folds' labels helped pick the columns, so chance agreement with them is built into the score
Because 5,000 columns are enough to learn anything
check.why: Out of 5,000 noise columns, the 20 that best match all 100 labels match the test rows too, by construction. Chosen inside each fold, they don't, and the score falls to a coin flip.

goals: Classify with k-nearest neighbors and choose k on held-out data
Run k-means step by step, and judge clusters honestly (inertia, silhouette, comparing with known labels)
Use a Gaussian mixture for soft clusters and a density
Flag anomalies by neighbor distance, density or an isolation forest, and say what a flag means
cards: Label a point by a vote of its k nearest labeled points; no training, all distance.
k = 1 memorizes noise (overfits); a very large k blurs everything (underfits). Choose k on validation data.
Repeat: assign each point to the nearest center, move each center to the mean of its points.
Sum of squared distances from points to their cluster centers; always falls as k grows.
k-means can end in a worse clustering from a bad start: run several starts, keep the lowest inertia.
Per point: how much closer to its own cluster than to the next one (−1 to 1).
Clusters describe the features you gave them, not the labels you hoped for.
Soft clusters with shapes: each point gets a probability per blob; fitted by EM, sized with BIC.
Random cuts isolate unusual points in few steps: few cuts = more anomalous.
A detector ranks the unusual; people decide what it means, and 'normal' drifts over time.

check.q: kNN with k = 1 scores 100% on its training rows and 59% AUC on new ones. What does that show?
options: Overfitting: each training row is its own nearest neighbor, so only held-out data measures it
A bug in the test set
kNN can't be used for classification
check.why: Use a larger k, chosen on validation data.

check.q: Which step of k-means moves the centers?
options: The move step: each center becomes the mean of the points assigned to it
Neither: centers stay where they started
check.why: Assign and move alternate until no point changes cluster.

check.q: Inertia keeps falling from k = 2 to k = 8 with no clear elbow. What should you conclude?
options: There may be no natural number of clusters: pick k by what's useful, and check what the clusters mean
k = 8 is best because inertia is lowest
check.why: Inertia always falls with k; the stations lie along lines, not in round groups.

check.q: What does a Gaussian mixture give that k-means doesn't?
options: Probabilities of belonging to each cluster, and clusters with their own shapes and tilts
check.why: It's a density: soft memberships, and a likelihood for every point (useful for anomalies).

check.q: An isolation forest flags a month-long elevator outage. What's the right reading?
options: It's unusual; a person checks whether it's an error or just rare (here: planned maintenance)
It's a data error and should be deleted
check.why: Anomaly scores rank the unusual; meaning comes from someone who knows the domain.

check.q: Why can a k-means step never increase the inertia?
options: Assigning moves each point to its nearest center, and the mean is the center with the smallest squared distances to its points
Because the number of clusters is fixed
Because the centers start at random points
check.why: Both moves can only shrink the sum of squared distances, and there are finitely many groupings, so the loop must stop, though maybe at a worse grouping than the best.

goals: Set one metric to optimize and turn the rest into limits
Diagnose avoidable bias, variance and data mismatch from human, training, train-dev and dev error, and pick the matching fix
Run an error analysis and compute each fix's ceiling
Read a learning curve to decide whether more data will help
cards: One number to beat; everything else (speed, size, false alarms) is a limit to meet.
A stand-in for the best possible error: the target for training error.
Training error − human-level: fix with a bigger model, longer training, better features, less regularization.
Train-dev error − training error: fix with more data, augmentation, regularization.
Held-out examples from the training source: separates variance from data mismatch.
Dev error − train-dev error: fix with training data that looks like real use.
Sort ~100 dev mistakes into categories before building anything.
Error × (1 − a category's share of mistakes): the lowest a perfect fix for that category can reach.
Training and validation error against training-set size: still falling means more data will likely help.
After tuning on it many times, dev looks better than test: get a fresh dev set.

check.q: Human-level 1%, training 1.5%, train-dev 7%, dev 7.5%. What's the main problem?
options: Variance: more data, augmentation or regularization
check.why: Bias 0.5, variance 5.5, mismatch 0.5 points.

check.q: Of 200 dev mistakes, 12 are blurry photos. Dev error is 10%. What's the most a perfect deblurring step could achieve?
check.why: 12/200 = 6% of the mistakes: 10% × 0.94 = 9.4%. A low ceiling: probably not worth weeks.

check.q: Validation error has stopped falling and sits close to training error, both well above human level. Will more data help?
options: Unlikely: the model itself has to change (it's bias, not variance)
check.why: Flat curves close together mean the model can't use more of the same data.

check.q: Why keep a train-dev set?
options: To tell variance (train-dev vs training) apart from data mismatch (dev vs train-dev)
check.why: Without it, a high dev error could be either, and the fixes are different.

check.q: You tuned 50 versions on the dev set. Dev error 4%, test error 6%. What happened?
options: You overfit the dev set by choosing what worked on it: get a fresh dev set
The model needs to be bigger
check.why: Each choice made on the dev set leaks a little of it into the model.

goals: Read A = UΣVᵀ as rotate, stretch, rotate, and find singular values with NumPy
Relate singular values to eigenvalues of AᵀA and to the condition number
Build the best rank-k approximation and judge how many layers to keep
Use the SVD for PCA, for filling in missing ratings, and for least squares (the pseudo-inverse)
cards: A = UΣVᵀ: rotate (Vᵀ), stretch along the axes (Σ), rotate (U). Every matrix has one.
The stretches σ₁ ≥ σ₂ ≥ … ≥ 0: the ellipse's semi-axes for a 2×2 matrix.
Singular values squared are the eigenvalues of AᵀA; its eigenvectors are V.
σ₁ / σ_min: how stretched the ellipse is, and how much errors get magnified.
Keep the k biggest layers σᵢuᵢvᵢᵀ: the closest rank-k matrix (Eckart–Young).
Σσᵢ² over the kept layers ÷ the total: how much of the matrix they hold.
SVD of the centered data: rows of Vᵀ are the components, σ²/(n−1) the variances.
A⁺ = VΣ⁺Uᵀ: invert each nonzero stretch; gives least squares and the smallest-norm answer.
Ratings ≈ people's tastes · films' qualities: a few hidden factors explain the table.
Fine-tune with ΔW = BA of rank r: 2·d·r trainable numbers instead of d².

check.q: What does the SVD say every matrix does to the plane?
options: Rotate, stretch along the axes, rotate
check.why: A = UΣVᵀ: Vᵀ rotates, Σ stretches, U rotates. Eigenvectors needn't exist or be at right angles.

check.q: Why do the singular values of A equal the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA?
options: Because ‖Av‖² = vᵀAᵀAv: the squared stretch along an eigenvector of AᵀA is its eigenvalue
Because A and AᵀA have the same eigenvectors for every A
Because singular values are defined as eigenvalues of A, and AᵀA squares them
check.why: Lengths of outputs are governed by AᵀA. A itself may have no real eigenvectors at all (a rotation), and A's eigenvalues are not its singular values unless A is symmetric.

check.q: A matrix has singular values 10 and 0.01. What does that tell you?
options: It's badly conditioned (condition number 1,000): solving with it magnifies errors
check.why: σ₁/σ₂ = 1,000: the ellipse is very thin.

check.q: Keeping the 20 biggest layers of a photo's SVD gives…
options: The closest possible rank-20 version of the photo
check.why: The Eckart–Young theorem: no rank-20 matrix is closer.

check.q: In the recommender, why do two singular values stand out?
options: The ratings were made from two hidden tastes, and the SVD found that the table is close to rank 2
check.why: A few big singular values mean a few hidden factors explain most of the table.

check.q: LoRA with rank 8 on a 4,096 × 4,096 layer trains how many numbers?
check.why: 2 × 4,096 × 8: two thin matrices whose product is the update.

goals: Compute surprise and entropy in bits, and read 2^H as "how many equally likely choices" (perplexity)
Explain entropy as the floor for compression, and why context lowers it
Compute cross-entropy and KL divergence, and explain why KL is never negative and why zeros make it infinite
Tell forward KL (covers) from reverse KL (chooses), and compute the information gain of a question
cards: −log₂ p bits: 1 bit for a coin flip, 10 bits for a 1-in-1,000 event.
H(p) = −Σ pᵢ log₂ pᵢ: the average surprise. 0 when certain, log₂ n when n outcomes are equally likely.
2^H (or 2^cross-entropy): as unsure as a choice among that many equally likely outcomes.
No code averages fewer bits than the entropy; context lowers the entropy. Predicting well = compressing well.
H(p, q) = −Σ pᵢ log₂ qᵢ: what you pay believing q when the truth is p. The training loss.
D(p‖q) = H(p, q) − H(p) ≥ 0: the extra bits of a wrong belief. Zero only when q = p.
A probability of 0 for something that happens costs infinite bits; smoothing and softmax avoid exact zeros.
D(p‖q) (maximum likelihood) makes the model cover all the data; D(q‖p) makes it choose one mode.
H(Y) − H(Y | X): the entropy a question removes. Decision trees split on the biggest one.
Fine-tuning with a reward adds β·D(new‖original) so the model can't drift into reward-gaming text.

check.q: A forecast gives four outcomes probabilities ½, ¼, ⅛, ⅛. Its entropy is…
check.why: ½·1 + ¼·2 + ⅛·3 + ⅛·3 = 1.75: the average number of yes/no questions with the best strategy.

check.q: Why can't any belief q beat the truth p on cross-entropy?
options: Because H(p, q) = H(p) + D(p‖q), and the KL divergence is never negative (ln x ≤ x − 1)
Because cross-entropy is symmetric in p and q
It can: a confident q can score below H(p)
check.why: The extra bits D(p‖q) are ≥ 0, with equality only at q = p. That's also why a training loss can't drop below the data's own entropy.

check.q: Your character model never saw "(" in training, and it appears in the test text. Its cross-entropy is…
check.why: Calling something impossible that then happens costs infinitely many bits. Adding 1 to every count (smoothing) fixes it.

check.q: Fitting one bell curve to two-humped data by maximum likelihood (forward KL) gives…
options: A wide bell covering both humps
A narrow bell on one hump
check.why: Forward KL punishes missing data most, so the fit covers both humps and puts weight in the empty middle. Reverse KL picks one hump.

check.q: A language model's held-out cross-entropy is 3 bits per token. Its perplexity is…
check.why: 2³ = 8 equally likely choices per token.

goals: Test a function for convexity with the chord picture, the second derivative and the Hessian's eigenvalues
Explain why a convex loss has no bad valleys, and why a network's loss isn't convex
Explain how an L2 penalty makes the best answer unique
Find the best point on a boundary with the Lagrange condition, and explain why L1 gives exact zeros
cards: Every chord stays on or above the curve: a bowl with no bumps (corners allowed).
In a convex function every valley bottom is the lowest point: gradient descent can't get trapped.
f″ ≥ 0; with many inputs, all Hessian eigenvalues ≥ 0. Sums, f(Xw) and maxima stay convex.
Linear regression (MSE) and logistic regression (cross-entropy), with or without L1/L2 penalties.
Relabeling hidden neurons gives equally good weights with a worse point between them.
λ‖w‖² adds 2λ to every curvature: a single lowest point, even with twin columns.
On a boundary g(w) = 0, the best point has ∇L = μ∇g: downhill points straight out.
μ: how much the best loss improves per unit of extra budget.
Max uᵀΣu with uᵀu = 1 gives Σu = μu: the best direction is an eigenvector.
L1's diamond has corners on the axes, so lasso gives exact zeros (feature selection); L2 only shrinks.

check.q: Why can't gradient descent get stuck in a bad valley of a convex loss?
options: If a lower point existed, the chord to it would put lower points right next to the valley bottom, so it wasn't a bottom
Because convex functions have no flat parts
Because convex losses are always quadratic
check.why: Every valley bottom of a convex function is the lowest point. Flat bottoms are possible, and convex losses come in many shapes (logistic, hinge).

check.q: A Hessian has eigenvalues 3, 0.5 and −0.2 at some point. The loss is…
options: Not convex: it curves down along one direction
Convex if the point is a minimum
check.why: Convex needs every eigenvalue ≥ 0 at every point; one negative curvature anywhere is enough to break it.

check.q: Why isn't a neural network's loss convex?
options: Relabeling two hidden neurons gives the same loss at different weights, and the point between them is worse
Because it uses too many weights
check.why: Equal ends with a bump in the middle is exactly what a chord test forbids. Kinks alone don't break convexity (|x| is convex).

check.q: Why does the L1 penalty give exact zeros while L2 doesn't?
options: The L1 budget is a diamond with corners on the axes, and the loss usually touches it at a corner
check.why: A smooth circle meets the loss where their directions match, almost never on an axis; a corner catches a whole range of losses.

check.q: At the best point on a constraint boundary, the loss's gradient is…
options: Parallel to the boundary's gradient (∇L = μ∇g)
check.why: Any part along the boundary would let you slide and improve; only the part straight across can remain.

goals: Predict the shape of any reduction or broadcast before running it
Tell views from copies, and avoid in-place changes leaking into the original
Turn a loop over numbers into array code, including every-pair tables
Write sums over indices with einsum and estimate an array's memory
cards: The direction a reduction uses up: axis=0 down the rows (one result per column), axis=1 across each row.
Keeps a reduced axis as size 1, so the result broadcasts back against the original.
Line shapes up from the right; each pair equal or one of them 1 (missing counts as 1); size-1 axes stretch.
Broadcasts to an n × n table: a wrong loss with no error. Assert shapes or .ravel().
Slices are views of the same memory; lists and masks copy. In-place changes through a view reach the original.
np.where(cond, a, b): an if on every item at once.
a[:, None] - b[None, :]: a column against a row gives the whole table of differences.
Name axes with letters; letters missing after -> are summed: 'ij,jk->ik' is A @ B.
Size × bytes per number: float64 8, float32 4, float16 2. 10⁶ × 10³ float32 = 4 GB.

check.q: X has shape (64, 10). What is the shape of X.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)?
check.why: Axis 1 is used up, and keepdims keeps it as size 1.

check.q: Which pair of shapes can NOT be broadcast together?
check.why: From the right: 3 vs 4, neither is 1. Use (4, 1) to subtract one number per row.

check.q: Why does broadcasting a (3,) array against a (1000, 3) one need no extra memory?
options: The stretched axis gets stride 0, so every row reads the same three numbers instead of copies
Because the result is computed lazily and never stored
check.why: Strides say how far to jump per index; a stride of 0 means 'the same number again'. (The result of A + B is stored, but B is never copied.)

check.q: v = X[10:20]; v[:] = 0. What happens to X?
check.why: A slice is a view of the same memory.

check.q: Which einsum computes a matrix times a vector?
check.why: j appears in both inputs and not after the arrow, so it's summed: Σⱼ Aᵢⱼ vⱼ.

check.q: About how much memory does a float32 array of 50,000 × 50,000 take?
check.why: 2.5 × 10⁹ numbers × 4 bytes = 10 GB: work in chunks instead.

goals: Load a real table and find its surprises with info, describe and value_counts
Filter, add columns, group, merge and pivot without silent mistakes
Use scikit-learn's fit/transform/predict contract to build and swap pipelines
Score with a time split and tune hyperparameters with a log-scale grid search
cards: df.info(), df.describe(), value_counts(), min/max of dates: before any model.
df[(cond1) & (cond2)]: brackets around each condition; & and | combine them.
df.loc[rows, columns] by label; write with it to change df itself.
Split by a key, apply a summary, combine: df.groupby('k')['v'].agg([...]).
'many_to_one' raises if the right table repeats a key, which would duplicate rows.
fit learns (attributes ending in _), transform and predict apply what was learned.
make_pipeline(prep, model): one estimator; cross-validation refits every step per fold.
Folds that train on the past and test on the next stretch of time.
Tries each setting with cross-validation; step__setting names a pipeline step's setting.
Try 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10: a penalty's effect depends on its order of magnitude.

check.q: Which filter keeps elevator outages longer than 4 hours?
check.why: & combines True/False columns row by row, and each comparison needs its own brackets.

check.q: f.groupby('reason')['hours'].mean() gives…
check.why: Split by reason, apply mean to each group's hours, combine into one row per reason.

check.q: Why can a merge silently make your counts wrong?
options: If the right table repeats a key, every matching left row is duplicated
Because merge drops columns with the same name
check.why: Each left row pairs with every matching right row. validate='many_to_one' or a row count check catches it.

check.q: Calling fit_transform on the test set is…
options: a leak: the scaler learns from test rows
the right way to prepare test data
check.why: fit learns; on test data only transform with what training taught.

check.q: Why use TimeSeriesSplit for the outages instead of shuffled folds?
options: The model will predict future outages, so each fold must train on the past and test on later data
Because the data has too few rows
check.why: A random split lets the model learn from outages after the ones it's tested on.

check.q: In a pipeline made by make_pipeline(prep, LogisticRegression()), how is C named for GridSearchCV?
check.why: The step's lowercase class name, two underscores, the setting.

goals: Explain why plain SGD crawls in a narrow valley and diverges above 2 / (steepest curvature)
Build momentum, RMSprop and Adam from the exponentially weighted average, with bias correction
Use AdamW and a warmup-plus-decay schedule in PyTorch
Search the learning rate on a log scale, with random points or a range test
cards: In a valley with curvatures λ, plain SGD diverges above η = 2/λ_max and crawls along the flat directions.
v ← βv + (1 − β)x: remembers about 1/(1 − β) recent values.
Divide an EWA that started at 0 by 1 − βᵗ; it matters only in the first steps.
Step along an EWA of gradients: zig-zags cancel, steady directions add up (about 1/(1 − β) times).
Divide each weight's step by the root of an EWA of its squared gradients: every weight moves about η.
Momentum + RMSprop + bias correction. Defaults β₁ 0.9, β₂ 0.999, η 1e-3.
Weight decay applied outside Adam's division, so every weight shrinks at the same rate.
Ramp the learning rate up over the first steps, while weights are random and Adam's averages unreliable.
Lower the rate along a half cosine toward 0, so late steps settle instead of bouncing.
Log scale (1e-4, 3e-4, 1e-3…), random points over a grid, or a range test.

check.q: A valley's steepest curvature is 50. Above what learning rate does plain SGD diverge?
check.why: Each step multiplies the steep error by 1 − 50η; past η = 2/50 that's below −1.

check.q: Why does momentum move faster along a valley's floor?
options: Gradients there point the same way every step, so the running average adds them up, about 1/(1 − β) times
Because it uses a larger learning rate
Because it ignores the gradient's size
check.why: g + βg + β²g + … = g/(1 − β): 10 times for β = 0.9. Across the valley the flipping signs cancel instead.

check.q: An EWA with β = 0.9 starts at 0 and sees the value 5 once. Without bias correction it says…
check.why: 0.9·0 + 0.1·5 = 0.5; dividing by 1 − 0.9 = 0.1 gives back 5.

check.q: What does RMSprop do that momentum doesn't?
options: Gives each weight its own step size, dividing by its typical gradient size
check.why: Momentum still has one η for everyone; RMSprop's √s is per weight.

check.q: Why AdamW instead of Adam plus an L2 penalty?
options: With Adam, the L2 term gets divided by each weight's √s, so heavily-updated weights barely decay
Adam can't use weight decay at all
check.why: AdamW subtracts ηλw outside the division: an even shrink.

check.q: Why warm up the learning rate at the start of training?
options: Early steps are the riskiest: random weights, big gradients, and Adam's averages based on very few steps
Because the loss is zero at the start
check.why: A small rate while the averages settle avoids a jump the model never recovers from.

goals: Explain vanishing and exploding signals as a per-layer factor raised to the depth
Choose He or Xavier initialization and say why He uses 2/n
Use batch norm, layer norm and dropout, and switch them correctly with train() and eval()
Diagnose a training run from its loss curves
cards: Each layer multiplies the spread by about the same factor; 0.9⁵⁰ ≈ 0.005, 1.1⁵⁰ ≈ 117.
Weights with variance 2/n_in for ReLU: the ReLU halves the energy, the 2 puts it back.
Variance about 1/n_in (averaged with n_out) for tanh-like bends.
Normalize each feature over the batch, then γx̂ + β; eval uses running averages saved in training.
Normalize each example over its features: same in training and use; transformers use it.
Zero each output with probability p while training, scale survivors by 1/(1 − p); off in eval.
y = x + f(x): the signal and the gradient always have a straight path.
Switches dropout off and batch norm to saved averages. Forgetting it is a classic deployment bug.
Nothing is learning: a bug in the loop, the data or the model.
Loss curve: training down, validation up
Overfitting: stop early, regularize, more data.

check.q: Why does He initialization use variance 2/n instead of 1/n for ReLU layers?
options: ReLU zeros the negative half, halving the signal's energy each layer; the 2 restores it
Because ReLU has a slope of 2
Because 2/n trains faster in every network
check.why: Var(z) = n·Var(w)·E[x²], and E[ReLU(z)²] = Var(z)/2. Keeping it steady needs n·Var(w)/2 = 1.

check.q: Each layer multiplies the signal's spread by 0.9. After 50 layers about how much is left?
check.why: 0.9⁵⁰ ≈ 0.005: depth turns small factors into huge ones.

check.q: Batch norm in eval mode normalizes with…
options: running averages of the mean and variance saved during training
the current batch's mean and variance
check.why: So one example at a time works, and gives the same answer every time.

check.q: Dropout with p = 0.2 scales the surviving outputs by…
check.why: So the expected total matches eval mode, where nothing is dropped.

check.q: Why do residual connections let much deeper networks train?
options: y = x + f(x) has derivative 1 + f′, so the gradient reaches early layers even when f′ is small
They remove the need for an optimizer
check.why: A plain stack multiplies many small factors; the residual's '1 +' gives a straight path.

check.q: The training loss sits at 2.30 from step 1 on a 10-class problem. Most likely…
options: the learning rate is too low
check.why: ln 10 ≈ 2.30 is the loss of uniform guessing. Try to overfit one batch to find the bug.

goals: Explain why GPUs win at matrix products and when work is compute-bound or memory-bound
Estimate a model's memory for inference and for training with Adam
Use mixed precision (autocast, bfloat16, loss scaling) and know what float16 breaks
Use gradient accumulation and choose a multi-GPU strategy
cards: An n×n by n×n product is 2n³ FLOPs (n³ multiplies, n³ adds).
FLOPs per byte moved. Above the GPU's balance (~150 on an A100) it's compute-bound; below, memory-bound.
Parameters × bytes: float16 2, 8-bit 1, 4-bit 0.5. 7B in float16 = 14 GB.
About 16 bytes per parameter (weights, gradients, m, s), plus activations.
Max 65,504, about 3 digits: overflows to inf, tiny gradients round to 0.
float32's range with about 2 digits: no loss scaling needed.
Multiply the loss before backward so small float16 gradients survive, divide after (GradScaler).
Backward on several micro-batches (loss ÷ count), then one step: a big batch's gradient in less memory.
Every GPU has the model and a slice of the batch; gradients are all-reduced (averaged) each step.
Split weights, gradients and optimizer state across GPUs when 16 bytes per parameter won't fit.

check.q: Why does a large matrix product run near a GPU's peak speed while a ReLU doesn't?
options: The product reuses each number fetched thousands of times; the ReLU does one operation per number and waits on memory
Matrix products use a different kind of memory
check.why: Arithmetic intensity: ~1,365 FLOPs per byte for a 4096² matmul vs ~0.25 for ReLU; the A100 needs ~156 to stay busy.

check.q: About how much memory does training a 1-billion-parameter model with Adam need, before activations?
check.why: About 16 bytes per parameter: weights, gradients and Adam's two averages.

check.q: In float16, the number 70,000 becomes…
check.why: float16's largest number is 65,504; past it is infinity.

check.q: Why does float16 training need a GradScaler but bfloat16 doesn't?
options: float16's small range turns tiny gradients into 0; bfloat16 has float32's range
GradScaler only works with float16 hardware
check.why: Scaling the loss lifts gradients above float16's underflow; bfloat16 never had the problem.

check.q: With gradient accumulation over 4 micro-batches, why divide each loss by 4?
options: So the summed gradients equal the gradient of the mean loss over the whole big batch
check.why: .backward() adds into .grad; four means each divided by 4 add up to one mean.

check.q: Data parallel on 4 GPUs with 64 examples each: the effective batch is…
check.why: Four gradients of 64 are averaged into one step.

goals: Explain why one run can't compare two close models, and compare averages over seeds instead
Make a run repeat exactly by seeding every source of randomness
Keep settings in configs and log every run with its code and data versions
Fingerprint data with a hash and save models together with how they were made

Average k seeds of each; the averages' spread shrinks by √k. Show the spread with the mean.
Seed random, NumPy and PyTorch (and the DataLoader's generator) to repeat a run exactly.
Parallel sums can differ in the last digit; torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True) forbids those kernels.
Every setting of a run in one dict or YAML, saved with the results.
One record per run: config, git commit, data hash, metrics, including failed runs.
A SHA-256 hash of the data file: one changed byte changes it completely.
Save weights with the config, data hash and metrics, so a model can be traced to how it was made.

check.q: Model B averages 1.1 points above model A, but each model's seed-to-seed spread is about 1.5 points. One run of each will…
options: often rank them the wrong way
check.why: Here A won about a quarter of single comparisons.

check.q: Why does averaging 10 seeds make a comparison more reliable?
options: The average's spread shrinks by √10 ≈ 3.2, so a real gap stands out from the noise
More seeds make the model more accurate
Because seed 10 is always the best
check.why: Spreads of averages fall like 1/√N (C4).

check.q: To repeat a PyTorch run exactly, you seed…
options: Python's random, NumPy, PyTorch and the DataLoader's shuffle
check.why: Every source of randomness, including the order of the data.

check.q: Why log failed and unremarkable runs too?
options: So you know how much searching produced the winner, and don't repeat dead ends
check.why: The best of many tries is optimistic; the count of tries says how much.

check.q: Why store a hash of the training data with each model?
options: If the data changes even slightly, the hash changes, so you know which data made which model
check.why: A fingerprint, not a copy: cheap to store, impossible to fake by accident.

check.q: Two runs with the same seed on a GPU end 0.2 points apart. Why?
options: Some GPU kernels add numbers in varying order, and floating-point addition isn't exactly associative
GPUs use random seeds of their own
check.why: Tiny differences grow over thousands of steps; deterministic algorithms remove them at some speed cost.

goals: Describe how vision networks grew from AlexNet to ResNet and MobileNet, and why stacked 3 × 3 filters win
Explain what early and late layers learn, and why early layers transfer
Choose augmentations that keep labels true
Use a pretrained network three ways: embeddings + a simple model, a new head on a frozen body, full fine-tuning
cards: Residual blocks + batch norm made 50–150-layer CNNs trainable (2015); ResNet-50: 76% ImageNet top-1 with 25.6 M weights.
Cheap depthwise convolutions: near-VGG accuracy with 3.5 M weights, small enough for phones and browsers.
Two see 5 × 5 with 18 weights instead of 25, plus an extra ReLU.
The patch of the input a neuron depends on; it grows with depth.
Early: edges and textures (general). Late: object parts and objects (task-specific).
Random label-preserving changes (crop, flip, color, rotation) every time a photo is seen; none at test time.
A pretrained body's output vector: photos that look alike land nearby.
Reuse a pretrained body; train only a small model or new head on your data.
Train all layers on new data at about a tenth of the usual learning rate, usually after the head has warmed up.

check.q: Why do VGG and ResNet stack 3 × 3 filters instead of using bigger ones?
options: Two 3 × 3 layers see a 5 × 5 patch with fewer weights (18 vs 25) and an extra ReLU in between
3 × 3 is the only size GPUs support
check.why: Three 3 × 3 layers see 7 × 7 for 27 weights instead of 49.

check.q: Which layers of an ImageNet network are most useful for a traffic-camera task?
options: The early and middle ones: edges, textures and parts are the same in any photo
None: ImageNet has no traffic cameras
check.why: Late layers are specific to ImageNet's classes; that's the part you replace.

check.q: Which augmentation would break a model reading street signs?
check.why: Mirrored text isn't the same sign; an augmentation must keep the label true.

check.q: Why can a frozen pretrained network plus logistic regression learn a new task from a few dozen photos?
options: The body already maps photos to vectors where similar photos are nearby; only a small model on top must be learned
Because logistic regression needs no data
Because pretrained networks know every category
check.why: 1,281 numbers to fit instead of millions: far less data needed.

check.q: Fine-tuning all layers of a pretrained network, you should use a learning rate that is…
options: much smaller than for training from scratch
larger, to change the weights faster
check.why: Big steps from a random new head would scramble the features you're borrowing.

goals: Explain a one-stage detector's output grid and which cell is responsible for an object
Encode a box as anchor offsets and log size ratios, and decode it back
Write a detection loss with box, objectness and class terms
Compute average precision, and score segmentation with Dice and IoU
cards: The image is cut into S × S cells; the cell containing an object's center is responsible for predicting it.
A few typical box shapes per cell (from k-means on training boxes); the network predicts corrections to the best-fitting one.
Center: σ(t) inside the cell. Size: anchor × eᵗ, so t = ln(w / anchor): relative errors, positive widths.
Each cell's probability that an object is centered there; trained everywhere, 1 only at responsible cells.
Box term (responsible cell only) + objectness (all cells) + class (cells with objects), weighted.
Area under each class's precision-recall curve over all confidence thresholds, averaged over classes (COCO: and over IoU 0.5–0.95).
Encoder shrinks (what), decoder grows back (where), skip connections carry sharp detail across matching levels.
2|P ∩ M| / (|P| + |M|) = 2·IoU / (1 + IoU); scores the class that matters, unlike pixel accuracy.

check.q: In YOLO, which cell predicts an object?
options: The one containing the object's center
The cell with the most of the object's pixels
check.why: One responsible cell per object keeps the targets unambiguous.

check.q: Why predict a box's width as ln(w / anchor) instead of w in pixels?
options: Errors become relative (twice too big costs the same at any size) and eᵗ keeps widths positive
Because logarithms are faster to compute
Because widths are always smaller than anchors
check.why: A 10-pixel miss matters on a bicycle and not on a bus; log ratios measure what IoU cares about.

check.q: In the detection loss, the box term is computed…
check.why: Empty cells have no box to describe; they learn 'no object' through objectness.

check.q: mAP differs from precision and recall at one threshold because it…
options: sweeps every confidence threshold and takes the area under precision-recall, averaged over classes
only counts the most confident box
check.why: It's chapter 12's PR curve, per class, summarized as an area.

check.q: Why do segmentation models report Dice or IoU instead of pixel accuracy?
options: When the class of interest covers few pixels, marking everything as background gets high accuracy but Dice 0
Pixel accuracy is hard to compute
check.why: The base-rate trap, per pixel.

goals: Write an RNN step and explain why one set of weights handles any length
Explain why gradients vanish or explode through time, and clip them
Explain how an LSTM's additive memory and gates keep gradients alive
Compare RNNs with transformers: parallel training, long-range links, cost per token
cards: h_t = tanh(W h_{t−1} + U x_t + b): the same weights at every step.
A fixed-size running summary of everything read so far.
Backprop through the unrolled loop: a deep network whose layers share weights.
Each step back multiplies the gradient by about the same factor: 0.9⁵⁰ ≈ 0.005.
Rescale the gradient when its length passes a limit (clip_grad_norm_): every RNN loop uses it.
A memory cell c_t = f⊙c_{t−1} + i⊙g, read through h_t = o⊙tanh(c_t); gates are sigmoids.
Start the forget gates open so the network begins by remembering.
Two gates and one state: a lighter LSTM, often about as good.
RNNs step in order (slow to train, constant cost per token); transformers run all positions in parallel.

check.q: Why can one RNN handle sequences of any length?
options: The same weights are applied at every step, feeding the state back in
It has a weight per position up to a maximum length
It reads the whole sequence at once
check.why: Like a convolution shares a filter over positions, an RNN shares one layer over time.

check.q: The gradient is multiplied by 1.1 at each step back. After 50 steps it has…
check.why: 1.1⁵⁰ ≈ 117: exploding gradients, which clipping keeps in check.

check.q: Why does an LSTM remember across long gaps better than a plain RNN?
options: Its cell is updated by addition, so going back a step multiplies the gradient only by the forget gate
It uses ReLU instead of tanh
check.why: ∂c_t/∂c_{t−1} = f_t: no matrix and no squash on that path.

check.q: Why start an LSTM's forget-gate bias at 1?
options: So the gates start mostly open and the memory (and its gradient) survives while the network learns what to forget
To make training faster per step
check.why: σ(1) ≈ 0.73 per bias, near 1 together: the network begins by remembering.

check.q: Why did transformers replace RNNs for most text work?
options: They train on all positions in parallel and link distant words directly
check.why: Recurrence forces step-by-step computation; attention is one big parallel matrix product.

goals: Compare characters, words and subwords as units of text
Build byte-pair encoding: count pairs, merge, train, encode new text
Explain UTF-8 bytes and why byte-level BPE never has unknown tokens
Explain token-driven failures: letter counting, digit arithmetic, per-language cost, glitch tokens

Start from characters (or bytes), merge the most frequent neighboring pair, repeat until the vocabulary is big enough.
Apply the learned merges in order; unseen words split into smaller pieces, never 'unknown'.
Characters as 1–4 bytes: English 1, Cyrillic 2, Chinese/Japanese 3, emoji 4.
More merges: shorter sequences, but bigger embedding and output layers.
The model sees 1–3 token ids, not 10 letters; letter counts are memorized, not seen.
English-centric tokenizers cut other languages into more tokens: higher cost, less context.
Merges frequent in the tokenizer's data but rare in the model's, so their embeddings are barely trained.
while condition: repeats its block as long as the condition is true; something inside must eventually make it false.

check.q: Why did subword tokenizers win over word-level ones?
options: They keep common words whole but can split any rare or new word into known pieces
They make every text shorter than words would
check.why: Word vocabularies explode and still miss new words; subwords cover everything.

check.q: Each BPE training step…
options: merges the most frequent neighboring pair into one new token
check.why: Greedy compression: the biggest saving first.

check.q: How many UTF-8 bytes is the Cyrillic word «Привіт» (6 letters)?
check.why: Cyrillic letters take 2 bytes each.

check.q: Why do chatbots struggle to count the r's in 'strawberry'?
options: They receive a few token ids, not individual letters, so the letters were never directly in their input
check.why: GPT-2 sees 'st', 'raw', 'berry', or one id for ' strawberry'.

check.q: The same question costs 3.7 times more tokens in Ukrainian than in English with GPT-2's tokenizer. Why?
options: The tokenizer learned its merges mostly from English text, so Ukrainian gets few multi-letter tokens
The API charges more for other languages
check.why: Fewer merges for a language means more, smaller pieces per word.

Train skip-gram with negative sampling and explain its loss
Find neighbors and solve analogies with cosine similarity, and know their limits
Measure biases in word vectors, and explain why one vector per word gave way to contextual embeddings
cards: You shall know a word by the company it keeps (Firth): shared contexts mean related meanings.
Predict a word's neighbors: σ(w·c) near 1 for real pairs, near 0 for random negative samples.
Contrast each real pair with K random words (drawn ∝ count^0.75) instead of scoring the whole vocabulary.
Randomly drop very frequent words (the, of) during training: they teach little.
At the optimum, w·c ≈ PMI(w, c) − ln K: word vectors are a low-rank summary of co-occurrence.
b − a + c, nearest word excluding a, b, c: king − man + woman ≈ queen.
Projections on he − she: nurse −0.33, captain +0.35 in GloVe; inherited from the training text.
word2vec/GloVe: one vector per word (bank = money bank). Transformers: a vector per word in context.

check.q: Why do 'cat' and 'dog' get similar vectors even if they rarely appear in the same sentence?
options: They appear with the same neighbors, and training pulls both toward those context vectors
They are near each other in the vocabulary list
check.why: Shared contexts, not co-occurrence with each other.

check.q: In skip-gram with negative sampling, each training example asks…
options: were these two words neighbors? (log loss on σ(w·c))
what is the next word? (softmax over the vocabulary)
how many times does this word appear?
check.why: A yes/no question per pair, with K random 'no' pairs for each real 'yes'.

check.q: king − man + woman, without excluding the input words, is closest to…
check.why: The sum stays nearest its starting point; analogy demos exclude the inputs.

check.q: In GloVe, man : doctor :: woman : ? returns 'nurse'. What does that show?
options: The vectors absorbed gender patterns from how the training text used these words
check.why: Embeddings compress their corpus's usage, stereotypes included: measure before building on them.

check.q: Why are the neighbors of 'bank' all about money?
options: One vector per word averages all its senses, dominated by the most frequent one in the training text
GloVe was trained only on finance news
check.why: Static vectors can't separate senses; contextual embeddings (transformers) do.

goals: Explain how a chat becomes one token sequence through a chat template, and why models are stateless
Write prompts that work: specific, instructions apart from data, named format, few-shot examples
Get reliable structured output: parse, validate, retry, constrain
Choose between hosted APIs and open weights, and estimate cost and latency in tokens

Every call resends the whole conversation; nothing is remembered between calls.
Worked input → output examples before the real input; the format becomes the likely continuation (in-context learning).
Ask for JSON, then parse, validate and retry; schema-constrained decoding guarantees it parses.
try: runs code that might fail; except SomeError: runs instead if it raises that error.
Fluent, confident, wrong: the likeliest continuation, not a looked-up fact. Ground facts in data or tools.
APIs: strongest models, per-token cost, data leaves. Open: control, privacy, pinned versions, your hardware.
n_in × p_in + n_out × p_out, prices per million; output costs several times more.
The prompt is read in parallel (compute-bound); output is one token at a time (memory-bound), so it's slower.

check.q: A chat has 20 turns. For the next reply, the model receives…
options: all 20 turns plus the new message, as one token sequence
a stored memory of the chat
check.why: Models are stateless; the app resends the history each call.

check.q: Why do two worked examples in the prompt make a small model's JSON so much more reliable?
options: After two question → JSON pairs, a third JSON answer is the most likely continuation
check.why: In-context learning: the same next-token prediction, steered by the pattern. In the notebook: 3/10 right → 9/10.

check.q: A program needs the model's answer as JSON. The robust approach is…
options: parse it, check the fields, retry on failure, and use schema-constrained output if available
trust it if the prompt says 'JSON only'
ask the model whether its answer is valid
check.why: Formats fail occasionally; code must check and recover.

check.q: When is an open-weights model the better choice?
options: When data must stay on your machines, the version must never change, or you want to fine-tune
check.why: Hosted APIs usually lead in quality; open weights win on control and privacy.

check.q: Why are output tokens slower and pricier than input tokens?
options: The prompt is processed in parallel, but each output token needs the previous one and rereads all the weights
Providers charge more for no reason
check.why: Decode is memory-bound, one token at a time; prefill is one big parallel matrix product.

goals: Explain sentence embeddings and how contrastive training turns meaning into distance
Build semantic, keyword and hybrid search and measure them with recall@k
Choose chunk sizes that an embedding model can read whole
Assemble a grounded RAG prompt with numbered, citable passages, and know retrieval's blind spots

In a batch of matching pairs, softmax over each row of cosines with the true pair as the answer: pull pairs together, push others apart.
Embed every piece once; embed the question; return the top-k cosines.
Keyword scores weighting words that are rare in the collection; perfect for exact terms and names.
Standardize keyword and embedding scores and add them: they fail on different questions.
Share of test questions whose answer appears in the top k results; measure at the k you pass to the model.
Split documents into pieces the embedding model reads whole (here ~100 words), with titles and overlap.
Retrieved passages, numbered, in the prompt: answer only from them, cite them, say if they don't say.
Approximate nearest-neighbor search (HNSW, FAISS) over millions of vectors in milliseconds.

check.q: Why can embedding search match a question to a passage that shares none of its words?
options: The model was trained to place texts with the same meaning close together, whatever words they use
It looks up synonyms in a dictionary
It can't: it needs shared words
check.why: Contrastive training on paraphrases and question-answer pairs.

check.q: Which query is keyword search better at than embedding search?
options: An exact identifier like an elevator id 'EL445X'
A question in different words than the document
check.why: Rare exact tokens carry little meaning for an embedding model but match perfectly as keywords.

check.q: Your RAG app sends the top 5 passages to the model. Which retrieval number matters most?
check.why: If the answer isn't in the five passages, the model can't use it.

check.q: Why did hybrid search beat both keywords and embeddings on the course's 35 questions?
options: They fail on different questions, so adding their standardized scores fixes some of each one's misses
Because it uses two models' worth of compute
Because the questions were written for it
check.why: 86% at k = 5 vs 77% and 80% alone.

check.q: Why does a RAG prompt tell the model to say when the passages don't contain the answer?
options: So a retrieval miss becomes an honest 'I don't know' instead of a fluent made-up answer
Because models can't read passages otherwise
check.why: Grounding fails sometimes; the instruction gives the model a way out.

goals: Choose between prompting, retrieval and fine-tuning for a need
Explain LoRA's low-rank update, its parameter count, and why B starts at zero
Prepare chat-formatted training data with the loss on the reply only
Test a fine-tune honestly (held-out data, new phrasings, general questions) and use switchable adapters
cards: More training on your examples, so a behavior becomes the default without being asked for.
Facts → retrieval (updatable, citable); behavior, format, style → fine-tuning.
W' = W + (α/r)·BA with B: d_out×r, A: r×d_in; only A and B train.
r(d_in + d_out) per matrix: 65,536 for rank 8 on 4096×4096 (0.4%).
So step 0 is exactly the pretrained model; A starts random so B's gradient isn't zero.
The frozen base stored in 4 bits, adapters in 16: a 7B fine-tune in a few GB.
Labels −100 on prompt tokens, so the loss is only on the reply.
A narrow fine-tune can overwrite general behavior: test general questions before and after.
Drop BA to get the original model back; serve many small adapters on one base.

check.q: Your bot must answer from this week's internal policies, which change often. Best tool?
options: Retrieval (RAG): passages update instantly and can be cited
Fine-tuning on the policies every week
A longer system prompt with every policy
check.why: Fine-tuning stores facts poorly and can't be patched line by line.

check.q: How many trainable numbers does a rank-4 LoRA add to a 1000 × 2000 matrix?
Why does LoRA initialize B to zero?
options: So the model starts exactly as the pretrained one and training begins from its real behavior
Because A would otherwise be unused
check.why: BA = 0 at step 0; A is random so B still gets a gradient.

check.q: Why set the labels of prompt tokens to −100 when fine-tuning a chat model?
options: PyTorch's cross-entropy skips −100, so the loss is only on the reply you want to teach
−100 marks the end of the text
check.why: Otherwise the model also learns to predict users' questions.

check.q: After a narrow fine-tune the model answers every question in the task's JSON format. A cheap fix that keeps the task's quality?
options: Keep the LoRA adapter separate and switch it on only for that task
Fine-tune again with a higher learning rate
check.why: Without BA the model is exactly the original.

goals: Build automatic checks for short answers (normalize, match, parse) and read their failures
Measure a grader's agreement with human labels using Cohen's kappa
Use model judges carefully: rubric, both orders, validated agreement
Grade faithfulness for RAG and compare system versions with paired tests and enough cases
cards: Fixed inputs with accepted answers or rubrics, from real use and past failures, rerun on every change.
Lowercase, strip punctuation and separators, then exact or whole-word containment checks.
(p_o − p_e)/(1 − p_e): agreement corrected for chance; 0 = chance, 1 = perfect.
A model grades replies against a rubric; validate its kappa against human labels first.
Position (test both orders), length, and self-preference.
Every claim in a RAG answer supported by the retrieved passages, graded apart from correctness.
Same questions for both versions; test the disagreements (exact binomial / McNemar).
20 cases: ±13 points; seeing a few points needs hundreds.
Test questions leaked into training data inflate scores; keep private, fresh sets.

check.q: Why can't you grade most LLM answers with exact string match?
options: The same correct answer can be phrased many ways, and exact match rejects all but one
check.why: 'ResNet-50 has 50 layers.' is right and doesn't equal '50'. Normalize and match whole words, or use a rubric.

check.q: A judge agrees with human labels 90% of the time, on a set where 90% of answers are correct. What do you know?
options: Nothing yet: an always-'correct' judge also gets 90%; check kappa
check.why: Raw agreement must be compared with chance agreement; kappa does that.

check.q: Why ask a pairwise judge in both orders?
options: Judges often favor a position; a verdict that flips with the order is position bias, not judgment
Because models read right to left
check.why: Count only verdicts that survive the swap, or average both orders.

check.q: A RAG answer is correct but adds a claim no passage supports. Which metric catches it?
check.why: Faithfulness asks whether every claim is grounded in the passages.

check.q: Version B beats version A on 4 questions and loses none, out of 20 shared questions. Conclusive?
options: No: the exact paired test gives p = 0.125; you need more questions
check.why: 2 × 0.5⁴ = 0.125. Small eval sets can't see small or even moderate differences.

goals: Wrap a model in an API that validates inputs and returns its version
Measure latency as percentiles and explain why tails dominate under fan-out
Tune dynamic batching's max batch and max wait for throughput vs latency
Use quantization and caching, and estimate the cost per prediction
cards: Load the model once, validate inputs against a schema, return the prediction and model version, expose a health check.
Serving builds features differently from training; share one preprocessing function.
p50, p95, p99: the median and the slow tail; report them, not the mean.
Fan-out to n calls makes 1 − 0.99ⁿ of requests hit a p99: 50 calls → 39.5%.
Collect requests up to a max batch or max wait, then run them together: fixed costs shared.
Weights in fewer bits with a scale per row: 8-bit lossless here, 4-bit nearly, 2-bit broken.
Return a stored answer when the input, model version and settings are identical; expire live data.
Machine price per hour ÷ predictions per hour; batching and scaling with traffic cut it.

check.q: Why does the service return a model version with every prediction?
options: So any bad prediction can be traced to the exact model that made it
check.why: Models change; logs must say which one answered.

check.q: Each of 10 backend calls is slow 1% of the time. About what share of pages hit a slow call?
Why does batching raise throughput so much?
options: Each run's fixed cost (launching, reading every weight) is shared by the whole batch
check.why: Time per batch ≈ t₀ + c·b: one at 21 ms, sixteen at 36 ms.

check.q: Raising dynamic batching's max wait from 5 ms to 30 ms at low traffic mostly…
options: raises latency while barely improving throughput
check.why: At low load batches can't fill anyway; requests just wait longer.

check.q: In the notebook, which weight precision broke the digit network?
check.why: 91.7% in float32 and 8-bit, 91.4% at 4-bit, 43% at 2-bit.

goals: Describe the production loop and what to monitor at each layer
Measure drift with PSI and choose reference windows that respect normal cycles
Ship new models safely: offline, shadow, canary, A/B, rollback
Build pipelines that validate data, gate on metrics and register models with model cards
cards: data → validate → train → evaluate → register → deploy safely → monitor, repeated.
Service and inputs and outputs now; outcomes (accuracy) when labels arrive, often late.
Inputs change vs the input-outcome relationship changes; only outcomes reveal the second.
Σ (p_live − p_ref) ln(p_live/p_ref): the symmetric KL between windows. <0.1 stable, >0.25 a real shift.
Weekly or yearly cycles look like drift; compare like with like.
The new model sees real requests and its answers are logged, not served.
A small share of traffic gets the new model while errors and outputs are watched.
The pipeline refuses to register a model below a floor or worse than the champion beyond noise.
The model's decisions shape the data it later trains on (blocked fraud is never labeled).

check.q: Labels for your model arrive three weeks late. What gives the earliest warning that something changed?
options: Input and prediction distributions, monitored every day
check.why: Inputs and outputs are available immediately; outcomes come last.

check.q: Why is PSI between Monday's and Saturday's data a poor alarm?
options: Weekly cycles make them differ every week; the alarm would fire on normal seasonality
check.why: On the outages: 0.32 weekday vs weekend, a 'real shift' that's just the weekly rhythm.

check.q: Inputs drifted (PSI 0.22), yet the model's AUC on the new data rose. What does that show?
options: Drift is a reason to look, not proof of damage; outcomes decide
check.why: Some shifts don't touch what the model relies on.

check.q: In a shadow deployment, users receive…
options: the current model's answers, while the new model's are only logged
check.why: Shadow tests on real traffic with zero user risk.

check.q: Why keep a small random slice of traffic unaffected by a fraud model?
options: The model hides outcomes of what it blocks; the slice shows the world it would otherwise never see
check.why: It breaks the feedback loop's blind spot.

goals: Carry a model from raw data to a monitored service, honestly evaluated
Recognize right-censored labels and build labels that respect them
Choose features known at prediction time and a threshold from stated costs
Document the model in a card and a one-page write-up
cards: Some durations are only known to be at least so long (still open); dropping them hides the long ones.
Open outages already past 4 h are labeled long; only open ones under 4 h are unknown.
Every feature must exist when the model decides: the first MTA estimate, not the latest revision.
Ship a simple model early, measure everything against it, keep it running.
A reason or station absent from training gets no weight: flag those predictions as low-confidence.
Kaplan–Meier and Cox models: the standard tools for censored durations.

check.q: 27% of finished outages lasted over 4 h, but 54% of open ones already have. Why does training only on finished outages mislead?
options: Long outages are the ones most likely to still be open, so dropping open ones under-represents them
check.why: Right-censoring: the snapshot catches long ones mid-way.

check.q: An open outage has lasted 9 hours. For the label 'over 4 hours', it's…
check.why: It has already passed 4 hours whatever happens next.

check.q: Why use only the MTA's first estimated return time as a feature?
options: Later revisions are made after the outage has dragged on: future information, i.e. leakage
The first estimate is always right
check.why: Ask of every feature: known at the moment of prediction?

check.q: Missing a long outage costs a rider 30 minutes, a needless reroute 5. The best threshold on P(long) is likely…
check.why: Misses are 6× worse, so say 'long' early (chapter 12's cost threshold).

check.q: What matters most in the capstone rubric?
options: Honesty of evaluation: time split, leakage and censoring handled, paired comparison with the baseline
check.why: A good model measured dishonestly is worth less than a modest one measured right.

goals: Decompose a series into trend, season, events and noise
Score forecasts against naive and seasonal naive baselines
Build lag, rolling and calendar features for a given horizon without leakage
Evaluate walk-forward, at the right horizon, with intervals checked for coverage
