Forecast = the same point one season ago (same weekday last week): the baseline to beat.
Correlation of a series with itself shifted by k: here 0.83 at 7 days, 0.49 at 1.
Values from k periods before, with k at least the forecast horizon.
Rolling stats for forecasting must end before the forecast moment; centered windows leak the future.
Train up to a date, test the next period, move on: many honest test windows.
How far ahead; errors grow with it, so evaluate at the horizon you'll use.
Check that a 90% interval really contains about 90% of outcomes on comparable periods.

check.q: Why does 'same weekday last week' beat 'same as yesterday' for subway ridership?
options: The weekly cycle is the strongest repeat (correlation 0.83 at lag 7 vs 0.49 at lag 1)
Last week's data is more accurate
check.why: Yesterday copies the wrong weekday effect: Monday after Sunday is off by a million.

check.q: For a forecast 7 days ahead, which feature leaks?
options: Riders 3 days before the forecast date
check.why: 3 days before isn't known yet when forecasting a week ahead.

check.q: Why shouldn't a forecasting model be evaluated with a shuffled train/test split?
options: It puts future days in training, so the test measures interpolation, not forecasting
check.why: Train on the past, test on what came after; walk forward.

check.q: A 90% interval built from summer errors covers only 59% of holiday-season days. Why?
options: Holiday errors are bigger than summer's; the interval was calibrated on a calmer period
check.why: Build intervals from comparable seasons and check coverage.

check.q: Which event would no feature built from past ridership have predicted?
options: The April 2020 collapse to about 0.4 million riders a day
check.why: Regime changes break forecasts; monitor and retrain.

goals: Predict ratings with matrix factorization: average, user and item biases, taste·traits
Explain why a few numbers per user and item suffice (low rank) and why regularization matters
Describe implicit feedback, two-tower retrieval and ranking, and ranking metrics
Recognize cold start, feedback loops and missing-not-at-random data
cards: r̂ = μ + b_u + b_i + p_u·q_i: biases plus a taste-traits match, learned from known ratings only.
How generous a user is, how good an item is overall: often most of the accuracy.
Tastes mix a few patterns, so k numbers per user and item fill a mostly empty table.
Clicks and plays instead of stars; trained to rank engaged items above sampled others.
User and item embedded separately; a vector index fetches candidates fast; a richer model ranks them.
Share of the items a user later engaged with that appeared in their top k.
New users or items have no vectors: use popularity, onboarding questions, content features.
Recommended items get the clicks that train the next model; reserve slots for exploration.

check.q: In r̂ = μ + b_u + b_i + p_u·q_i, what does b_i capture?
options: How well item i is rated by everyone, regardless of taste
check.why: Item bias: overall quality. μ is the global mean, p_u·q_i the personal match.

check.q: Why can a few taste numbers per person fill a table that's 98% empty?
options: Tastes mix a few patterns, so the full table is approximately low-rank: far fewer unknowns than known ratings
Because empty cells are filled with zeros
Because the model memorizes the table
check.why: k(m + n) numbers instead of m·n cells.

check.q: Without a penalty, 16-factor MF on MovieLens did no better than predicting the average. Why?
options: The taste vectors fit the noise in the training ratings (overfitting)
check.why: 0.90 RMSE vs 0.91 for the mean; with a strong penalty 0.83.

check.q: A brand-new user has no ratings. Matrix factorization alone can recommend…
options: roughly the items good for everyone (μ + b_i)
check.why: Cold start: no taste vector yet. Ask, or use context and content.

check.q: Why is recall@10 on last month's clicks an imperfect test of a new recommender?
options: Those clicks were shaped by the old recommender's choices; only an A/B test shows if users are better off
Recall can't be computed on clicks
check.why: Offline data reflects what was shown, not what users would have chosen.

check.q: Why can a model with the best rating RMSE still make a worse top-10 list than plain popularity?
options: Predicting stars rewards obscure items with a few high ratings; ranking what a user will engage with is a different objective
check.why: In the notebook: recall@10 0.7% for the RMSE-trained model vs 3.6% for most-rated. Train on the ranking itself.

goals: Define agent, state, action, reward and the discounted return
Explain the Bellman equation and how values flow backward from rewards
Implement Q-learning with ε-greedy exploration
Explain policy gradients, RLHF, and why RL is hard (sparse rewards, instability, reward hacking)
cards: G = r₁ + γ r₂ + γ² r₃ + …: future rewards, each step discounted by γ.
How much the future counts: 0.95⁵⁰ ≈ 0.077; low γ makes the agent short-sighted.
Q(s, a) = E[r + γ max Q(s′, a′)]: values agree with themselves one step later.
Q(s, a) += α [r + γ max Q(s′, ·) − Q(s, a)] after every step.
Random action with probability ε, else the best known: exploration so better paths can be found.
Raise log π(a|s) in proportion to the return that followed; normalize returns to cut noise.
A reward model learned from human preference pairs; the language model tuned with PPO to score well on it.
The agent optimizes the reward as written, not as meant (the boat that circles forever).

check.q: Rewards −1, −1, +10 with γ = 0.9 give a return of…
Why does the Bellman equation let value 'flow backward' from the goal?
options: Each state's value is defined by the next state's value, so updates near the reward propagate to earlier states
check.why: Q(s, a) = r + γ max Q(s′, ·): neighbors of the goal learn first, then theirs.

check.q: Why does Q-learning need exploration (ε > 0)?
options: Without it, the agent keeps repeating the first path that worked and never discovers better ones
To make training faster per step
check.why: Greedy-only agents get stuck with early habits.

check.q: In RLHF, what plays the role of the reward?
options: A reward model trained to predict which of two answers people prefer
check.why: Human preference pairs → reward model → PPO on the language model.

check.q: An agent rewarded for hitting targets circles them forever instead of finishing the race. This is…
options: reward hacking: it optimized the reward as written
check.why: Design rewards for what you mean, and watch the behavior.

goals: Describe the forward process and the noise schedule
Explain the training objective: predict the added noise at every level
Explain sampling as many small denoising steps from pure noise
Explain text conditioning, classifier-free guidance, latent diffusion, and memorization
cards: x_t = √ᾱ_t x₀ + √(1 − ᾱ_t) ε: image blended with noise on a fixed schedule.
Product of the per-step α's: the share of variance that's still image after t steps.
Train ε_θ(x_t, t) with MSE to the added noise; knowing the noise gives the clean image.
Start from pure noise and denoise step by step (DDPM, or 20–50 steps with DDIM).
ε = ε_uncond + w(ε_cond − ε_uncond); higher w follows the prompt more, with less variety.
Image patches attend to the prompt's text embeddings.
Diffuse in an autoencoder's compressed latent (e.g. 48× fewer numbers), decode at the end.
An ideal denoiser reproduces training points; real networks generalize, but can copy repeated images.

check.q: What does a diffusion model's network learn to predict?
options: The noise that was added to an image at a given step
check.why: MSE between true and predicted noise, at every noise level.

check.q: Why can training jump straight to step t without walking the whole noise chain?
options: Independent Gaussian noises add up to one Gaussian, so x_t has a closed form from x₀
Because the network remembers earlier steps
check.why: Variances add: x_t = √ᾱ_t x₀ + √(1 − ᾱ_t) ε.

check.q: Raising the classifier-free guidance scale w from 1 to 3 makes samples…
options: follow the prompt more strictly, with less variety
check.why: In the notebook: 97% → 100% read as the requested digit, variety (pixel spread) 0.30 → 0.24.

check.q: Why does latent diffusion run much faster than diffusion on pixels?
options: It denoises a compressed latent with far fewer numbers (48× fewer for 1024² images into 128²×4)
check.why: Every denoising step works on the small latent; a decoder makes pixels once at the end.

check.q: Why did the page's 2-D sampler produce only copies of its training points?
options: Its denoiser was the exact best one for those points, which reproduces them; real networks can't represent that and generalize
Because it used too few steps
check.why: Memorization is the ideal denoiser's behavior; capacity limits are part of why models generalize.

goals: Describe audio as samples and the sampling rates speech uses
Build a log-mel spectrogram: frames, Fourier transform, mel bands, log
Train a CNN on spectrograms and test it on unseen speakers
Explain wake-word trade-offs (false accepts per hour vs misses) and Whisper's design
cards: Measurements per second: 8 kHz phone, 16 kHz speech models, 44.1 kHz music.
Short overlapping windows, each Fourier-transformed: frequency over time, an image.
Dot products with sines: a change of basis from time to frequency; the FFT does it in n log n.
Frequency bands spaced like hearing: narrow low, wide high.
The log of mel-band energy per frame: the standard input of speech models.
Hold out whole speakers: 97% random split vs 79% on an unheard voice in the notebook.
An encoder-decoder transformer: 30 s of 80-band log-mel in, text tokens out.
How often a wake-word detector fires on background audio; judged with the miss rate.

check.q: One second of audio at 16 kHz is how many numbers?
check.why: 16,000 samples per second.

check.q: Why use the mel scale for speech features?
options: It spaces frequency bands like human hearing, which distinguishes low pitches finely and high ones coarsely
check.why: Fewer, perceptually sensible bands; speech information sits where hearing resolves well.

check.q: Why does a Fourier coefficient pick out its own frequency and ignore others?
options: Sines of different frequencies are perpendicular, so the dot product with the signal keeps only the matching part
Because it filters with a neural network
check.why: A change to a perpendicular basis, as in linear algebra 2.

check.q: A spoken-digit model scores 97% on a random split and 79% on a new speaker. Why the gap?
options: The random split put the test speaker's voice in training: a group leak
check.why: Split by speaker, like GroupKFold in features and leakage.

check.q: How should a wake-word detector's false alarms be reported?
options: False accepts per hour (or day) of background audio, next to the miss rate
As the share of wake words detected
check.why: It checks ~100 times a second all day; 'almost always right' can still mean many false wakes.

goals: Explain encoder-decoder models and teacher forcing
Explain the one-vector bottleneck and how attention removed it
Compare greedy, beam search and sampling, including length normalization
Compute BLEU and know what it misses
cards: An encoder reads the input into vectors; a decoder writes the output token by token, conditioned on them.
In training, the decoder gets the correct previous token at every step, not its own guess.
At each output step, a weighted average of all encoder vectors, weights from the decoder state: the origin of attention.
Always the most likely next token: fast, can lead into a poor overall sequence.
Keep the k best partial sequences by total log-probability; width 1 is greedy.
Rank by log-probability per token (or length^α), since totals always favor short outputs.
Clipped n-gram precisions (1–4) against references, geometric mean, brevity penalty.
Trained on correct histories, generating from its own; early mistakes compound.

check.q: What problem did attention originally solve in translation?
options: The encoder squeezed the whole sentence into one vector, so long sentences lost information
check.why: Attention lets each output step read all encoder vectors directly.

check.q: What is teacher forcing?
options: Feeding the decoder the correct previous token during training
Forcing the model to output the reference
check.why: It trains every position in parallel from the right history, at the cost of exposure bias.

check.q: Why does beam search tend to prefer short outputs without length normalization?
options: Every extra token adds a negative log-probability, so totals fall with length
check.why: Divide by length (or length^α) to compare fairly.

check.q: For open-ended story writing, which decoding is usually best?
options: Beam search with a wide beam
check.why: The single most likely text is bland and repetitive; sampling gives variety.

check.q: A correct paraphrase gets a low BLEU score. Why?
options: BLEU counts exact n-gram overlap with the reference, not meaning
check.why: Use BLEU across many sentences, and humans or judges for meaning.

goals: Explain verification and identification with embeddings and a distance threshold
Train an embedding with triplet loss and test it on identities never seen
Measure false accepts and false rejects, overall and per group, and know the legal and ethical context
Explain neural style transfer: content features, Gram-matrix style, gradient descent on pixels
cards: Same person? (distance below a threshold) vs who is it? (nearest embedding in a database).
Two or three inputs through the same network with shared weights, trained on their distances.
max(0, |a − p|² − |a − n|² + m): positives closer than negatives by a margin.
Embeddings generalize to unseen identities only when trained on many: Omniglot 0.96 AUC; 8 digits not enough.
Impostors let in vs genuine users refused; a threshold trades one for the other.
NIST 2019: false positive rates varied by 10–100× across groups for many algorithms.
Channel-by-channel feature correlations summed over positions: texture without layout.
Optimize the pixels to keep a photo's deep features and match a painting's Gram matrices.

check.q: Why can't face recognition be an ordinary classifier over people?
options: New people appear constantly with one or two photos; an embedding compared by distance handles anyone
check.why: Verification compares embeddings; no retraining per new person.

check.q: Raising the verification threshold (allowing larger distances) mostly…
options: raises false accepts and lowers false rejects
check.why: More pairs count as 'same': impostors get in, owners are refused less.

check.q: An embedding trained with triplet loss on only 8 digits did worse than raw pixels on the 2 unseen digits. Why?
options: With few identities it learns to separate those classes, not what 'same' means in general
check.why: On Omniglot's 964 training characters it generalizes to unseen ones (0.96 AUC).

check.q: Before deploying face verification with a 0.1% average false accept rate, what must be checked?
options: False accept and false reject rates per demographic group
check.why: One threshold can spread errors unevenly; NIST found large differentials.

check.q: Why does a Gram matrix capture style but not content?
options: It sums feature co-occurrences over all positions, so it keeps which textures appear together and loses where
It only uses the first layer
check.why: Shuffle the positions and the Gram matrix doesn't change.

goals: Explain least squares as minimizing the total of squared misses, and solve it with the normal equation
Tell what ridge and lasso penalties do to weights, and pick between them
Spot where a line breaks: bends, outliers, near-duplicate columns and trends past the data
cards: Pick the weights that make the sum of squared residuals smallest; big misses dominate.
XᵀX w = Xᵀy: the residuals end up perpendicular to every column.
Adds λ·Σw² to the loss: every weight shrinks, twins share the credit evenly.
Adds λ·Σ|w|: the soft threshold sets the least useful weights to exactly zero.
Near-duplicate columns make weights huge and unstable while predictions stay the same.
A line keeps its trend past the data; trees go flat. Either can be wrong.

check.q: Least squares minimizes…
options: the number of points off the line
the total of the squared vertical misses
the distance from the points to the origin
check.why: The total area of the squares on the residuals.

check.q: Why does one far-off point pull a least-squares line so much?
options: Its miss is squared, so shrinking it is worth making every other point a little worse
The line must pass through every point
check.why: A miss of 3 costs 9; absolute or Huber loss grow slower.

check.q: In the normal equation's solution, the residuals are…
options: perpendicular to every column of X
check.why: Xᵀ(y − Xw) = 0: if they leaned toward a column, more of that column would shrink them.

check.q: You want a model that uses only a few of 200 columns. Which penalty?
check.why: Lasso's absolute value pulls weights to exactly zero.

check.q: Two columns are near copies. Plain least squares gives them weights +3.5 and −3.0. What's true?
options: The predictions are fine, but the weights can't be read
One column should be +3.5 in reality
check.why: Only their sum matters to predictions; ridge or dropping a twin makes the weights meaningful.

goals: Explain logistic regression as a straight edge whose distance becomes a probability
Read a weight as an odds ratio and check calibration
Recognize where it breaks: bent edges, perfect separation, unscaled or twin columns, rare classes
cards: p = σ(w·x + b): a weighted sum squashed into a probability.
ln(p / (1 − p)); logistic regression says it's a weighted sum of the columns.
e^w: how much one more unit of a column multiplies the odds of a yes.
Predicted chances match real rates: of calls given 20%, about 20% say yes.
When a column splits the classes completely, the unpenalized weight grows forever.
Add x², y², x·y and a straight edge in those columns can be a circle on the plane.

check.q: Logistic regression's decision boundary on the original two columns is…
check.why: p = 0.5 where w·x + b = 0: a straight line, unless you add columns.

check.q: A weight of 0.7 on a 0/1 column means a yes is…
check.why: Weights add to log-odds, so they multiply the odds by e^w.

check.q: Why are logistic regression's probabilities usually well calibrated?
options: At the log-loss minimum, predictions add up to the real counts in every group the columns describe
They aren't; they need a separate fix
check.why: The gradient is Σ(p − y)x = 0, column by column.

check.q: Your logistic regression has one weight of 380 and predicts exactly 0 or 1. Most likely…
options: a column separates the classes perfectly, maybe a leak, and there's no penalty
the learning rate is too small
check.why: On separable data the unpenalized weight runs off to infinity.

check.q: On 10,000 bank calls, logistic regression scored AUC 0.78 and boosted trees 0.76. The best reading is…
options: with mostly additive effects and modest data, a line is as good as anything, and it's readable
check.why: Always fit the simple baseline: it often ties.

goals: Explain kNN as a vote among the k closest training points, and choose k on validation data
Show why scaling and useless columns decide what 'nearest' means
Recognize the curse of dimensionality and kNN's prediction cost
cards: Store the training rows; predict by the vote of the k closest ones.
Small k: detailed and noisy; large k: smooth and biased to the majority. Pick on validation data.
Every column adds to the distance in proportion to its numbers; scale so units don't decide.
The error even the true probabilities can't avoid; 1-NN is at most twice it, with lots of data.
In many columns, the nearest and farthest points are about equally far.
No training cost, all the cost at prediction: it scans (or indexes) the stored data.

check.q: With k = 1, training accuracy is…
options: 100%, since each point is its own nearest neighbor
check.why: k = 1 memorizes; validation shows the noise it copied.

check.q: Why does a column measured in big numbers hurt kNN?
options: Its squared differences dominate the distance, whatever the column means
check.why: Distance sums each column's squared difference; scale the columns first.

check.q: What does fitting a kNN model do?
check.why: All the work happens at prediction time.

check.q: With 1,000 columns, the nearest of 1,000 random points is about 0.9 times as far as the farthest. What does that mean for kNN?
options: 'Nearest' barely means anything, so the vote is close to random
check.why: The curse of dimensionality: reduce columns or learn a better distance (embeddings).

check.q: Digits plus 640 noise columns: kNN 48%, logistic regression 86%. Why the difference?
options: Logistic regression learns small weights for noise; kNN's distance counts every column
check.why: A distance can't learn which columns matter.
